title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
In this analysis, I look at how many households that received SNAP assistance with income were below poverty levels in the past 12 months across counties in California, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                          estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                            <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Sierra County, California           13    17   131. 
 2 Mono County, California            104   101    97.1
 3 Alpine County, California           14    11    78.6
 4 Trinity County, California         161    95    59.0
 5 Plumas County, California          378   192    50.8
 6 Modoc County, California           225    98    43.6
 7 Glenn County, California           296   127    42.9
 8 Amador County, California          525   225    42.9
 9 Colusa County, California          315   135    42.9
10 San Benito County, California      447   190    42.5


The least reliable county appears to be Sierra County, California with a moe_pct of 130.8%. The margin of error is larger than the estimate itself so the true number of poverty-level SNAP households is obscured.

county_data <- county_data %>%

count(county_data, reliability)

1 High confidence     3
2 Low confidence     41

  1.600   9.117  14.917  23.245  27.842 130.769 

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 25 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))
  
count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    17
2 Low confidence     16
3 Moderate           25


I set the cutoffs at 10% and 25% instead of the default 5% and 10%, based on the quantiles. The original thresholds pushed 41 of 58 counties into “Low confidence”, but these new cutoffs roughly split counties into thirds. I chose 10 and 25 because it was closer to the actual quartiles and I played around with the numbers to test it out. It’s worth noting that the distribution is right-skewed with a small number of very small counties like Sierra County pulling the average up.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 06001 Alameda County, California    18830   1141 1651949    NA
2 06003 Alpine County, California        14     11    1695   234
3 06005 Amador County, California       525    225   41029    NA
4 06007 Butte County, California       5768    579  209470    NA
5 06009 Calaveras County, California    556    207   45995    NA
6 06011 Colusa County, California       315    135   21895    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence          3       5193699 
2 Low confidence          29         93740.
3 Moderate                26        805508.


High confidence counties have an average population of around 5.2 million, compared to roughly 94,000 for lower confidence counties. Larger populations have larger ACS samples which help to produce smaller relative margins of error. Reliable SNAP-poverty estimates are likely only available for three of California ’s largest counties.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
The communities in California that we know least about include: Sierra, Mono, Alpine, Trinity, Plumas, Modoc, Glenn, Amador, Colusa, and San Benito. Sierra has a margin of error percentage of 130.8%, indicating that the estimate of 13 households has a margin of error larger than the number itself.
The communities of Mono and Alpine are also in the lower confidence bracket, likely due to the relatively lower average population. Communities with a higher average population place higher in confidence levels. The ACS is an ongoing sample survey across five years to build the estimates that we examine. Only a select few households are sampled for a given area, but the number of households with data increases as the population count rises. Los Angeles County will have more samples when compared to Sierra County, because the latter will have only a handful of survey respondents that even fall into the subpopulation of households with SNAP and below the poverty level.
If every county’s number were to be treated as equally certain during funding allocation, smaller counties are likely to feel greater harm because these estimates are sensitive to sampling noise. Year to year, the numbers for a large population county like Los Angeles will budge slightly because the sample is large enough to average out the noise. However, a small county’s number is more likely to swing which could affect their funding despite need still being great.

title: Verify the Claim: Changing poverty rates in Philadelphia’s Neighborhoods
text:
In this analysis, I will examine the 2018 WHYY article “New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty.” The article claims that Eastwick, Philadelphia “showed the greatest poverty-rate increase of any community,” rising from 12 percent in the 2006–10 American Community Survey to 26 percent in the 2013–17 survey. To test this, I measure poverty rate using 5-year ACS B17001_002 (population with income in the past 12 months below the poverty level) and B17001_001 (population for whom poverty status is determined). The ACS5 publishes at the census tract level while the 1-year ACS are limited to geographies above roughly 65,000 people.
Since the article does not specify which tracts went into the neighborhood of Eastwick’s analysis, I pulled poverty rate data for every census tract in Philadelphia County and checked where a tract-level increase on the scale the article reports (14%) falls relative to the rest of the city, instead of assuming my own boundaries for Eastwick. Thus, my analysis will focus on the magnitude of the claim and test whether an increase that large is exceptional somewhere in Philadelphia, but it cannot confirm that the tract producing the largest increase is actually in the article’s Eastwick. The two periods of 2006–10 and 2013–17 do not share underlying survey years which provides a better before and after comparison. Any statistically significant difference will reflect real change over time.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Pulling data


Show code
get_phl_poverty <- function(yr) {
  get_acs(
    geography = "tract",
    state     = "PA",
    county    = "Philadelphia",
    variables = c(below_poverty = "B17001_002", total = "B17001_001"),
    year      = yr,
    survey    = "acs5",
    output    = "wide"
  ) %>%
    mutate(
      share     = below_povertyE / totalE,
      share_moe = moe_prop(below_povertyE, totalE, below_povertyM, totalM),
      period    = paste0(yr - 4, "-", yr)
    )
}

phl_poverty <- bind_rows(
  get_phl_poverty(2010),
  get_phl_poverty(2017)
)

title: Verify the Claim: Changing poverty rates in Philadelphia’s Neighborhoods
text:
Computing change


Show code
phl_wide <- phl_poverty %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, share, share_moe) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = c(share, share_moe))

phl_tested <- phl_wide %>%
  mutate(
    change      = `share_2013-2017` - `share_2006-2010`,
    se_1        = `share_moe_2006-2010` / 1.645,
    se_2        = `share_moe_2013-2017` / 1.645,
    se_diff     = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff    = se_diff * 1.645,
    z           = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(significant)) 

phl_tested %>% count(significant)


# A tibble: 2 × 2
  significant     n
  <lgl>       <int>
1 FALSE         313
2 TRUE           63


Of the 376 tracts with a defined poverty rate in both periods, only 17% (63 tracts) show a change large enough to be statistically distinguishable from zero at 90 percent confidence. The remaining 83% have low apparent difference between the two periods that is small enough and could be sampling noise

title: Verify the Claim: Changing poverty rates in Philadelphia’s Neighborhoods
text:
Verdict: Not Supported
The claim that Eastwick posted “the greatest poverty-rate increase of any community” in Philadelphia is not supported. Because Eastwick’s constituent tracts are not published, this analysis tested the claim’s magnitude across every valid Philadelphia tract instead to find that 63 tracts show a statistically significant change. Some of the largest raw changes, however, come from tracts too small to produce a reliable estimate.
Census Tract 9800 appeared to swing by nearly 79 percentage points, but its 2013–2017 estimate carries a coefficient of variation of 85.6 percent, which is more than double the 40 percent threshold Jurjevich et al. (2018) classify as unreliable. The number is likely an artifact of a small, unstable sample rather than a genuine change. An online search reveals that Census Tract 9800 primarily covers Fairmount Park west of the Schuylkill River. Census Tract 56’s 35.7-point increase is a closer call, with a coefficient of variation of 40.2 percent, and should possibly be evaluated as borderline rather than dismissed outright the way Tract 9800’s figure could be.


# A tibble: 2 × 4
  NAME                                                change_pct cv_0610 cv_1317
  <chr>                                                    <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1 Census Tract 56, Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania        35.7    40.2    20.9

title: Verify the Claim: Changing poverty rates in Philadelphia’s Neighborhoods
text:
Revisiting the article
The new Census data showed poverty rising sharply in some parts of Philadelphia, though not evenly across the city. Of Philadelphia’s roughly 380 census tracts, about one in six saw a poverty rate change between 2006–10 and 2013–17 large enough to rule out ordinary survey noise. That likely means an increase on that scale is real and consistent with a broader citywide pattern, even though which specific tracts make up “Eastwick” isn’t public data. One tract even rose more than 30 percentage points, so Eastwick’s reported increase falls in the middle of a wider group of Philadelphia tracts experiencing comparably large or larger changes (some rising and some falling) over the same period. For policymakers, it is evident that multiple areas of the city are seeing statistically significant poverty increases.

The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}

text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}



Finding a table name
On a dataset’s OpenDataPhilly page, look for the API link. The table name is the word after FROM in the example query. To see what values a column takes before you filter on it, ask for a count in CSV format:

text:
Part 4: Building spatial features
Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

4A: Counting
How many burglaries fall in each tract?


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary)))

summary(tracts$n_burglary)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  0.000   4.000   7.000   9.446  13.000  48.000 


A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,   # sq ft in a sq mile
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    burglary_per_1k   = n_burglary / total_popE * 1000
  )








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.


Code
stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)   # always inside the tract, unlike a centroid

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, stations)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)




4D: Measuring distance to one place
Sometimes the “thing” is a single location, such as City Hall as a stand-in for the center of the regional economy.


Code
city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)) / 5280)




4E: Your turn
Build at least three spatial features from your own layers, and use at least two types (count, density, nearest distance, distance to a place). After each one, fit a model, cross-validate it, and log it.

tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)

rail_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, layer1)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_rail_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, layer1[rail_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)

  add_row(model = "m2", added = "distance to nearest rail station",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f2, tracts),
          notes = "Regional Rail + MFL + BSL stations, from point on surface")

# feature 2: food business density
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    n_food = lengths(st_intersects(geometry, layer2)),
    area_sqmi = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) / 27878400,
    food_per_sqmi = n_food / area_sqmi
  )

f3 <- update(f2, . ~ . + food_per_sqmi)

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m3", added = "food business density",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f3, tracts))

# feature 3: distance to nearest trolley stop
trolley <- st_read("https://opendata.arcgis.com/api/v3/datasets/dd2afb618d804100867dfe0669383159_0/downloads/data?format=geojson&spatialRefId=4326", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

trolley_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, trolley)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_trolley_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, trolley[trolley_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)

f4 <- update(f3, . ~ . + dist_trolley_mi)

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m4", added = "distance to nearest trolley stop",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f4, tracts),
          notes = "SEPTA trolley stations 2023")

model_log %>%
  mutate(change = cv_rmse - lag(cv_rmse))


# A tibble: 4 × 5
  model added                            cv_rmse notes                    change
  <chr> <chr>                              <dbl> <chr>                     <dbl>
1 m1    ACS baseline                       11.2  renter share, log densi… NA    
2 m2    distance to nearest rail station   10.9  Regional Rail + MFL + B… -0.352
3 m3    food business density              10.0  <NA>                     -0.852

Answer: Which spatial feature helped most? Did any feature you expected to help do nothing, or make CV RMSE worse? Why might that be?
Food business density helped most and cut CV RMSE by about 0.85 percentage points. Together, the three spatial features brought the error from 11.2 to 9.4 points. There wasn’t a feature that made the model worse, but distance to rail helped less than I expected (−0.35). However, rail stations are concentrated in areas the baseline already accounts for, and many Regional Rail stations sit in neighborhoods like Chestnut Hill so being near a station doesn’t necessarily mean living without a car. Food business density gives a better idea of where groceries, corner stores, and restaurants are within walking distance, which helps residents live without a car for basic needs. Trolley distance also helped substantially (−0.62), likely because trolley lines run through neighborhoods in West and Southwest Philadelphia where the baseline had underpredicted. Since each feature was added on top of the previous ones, these gains depend on order.

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()















Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.


Code
m_sq <- lm(y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)
summary(m_sq)

Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)
Answer in prose, drawing on your model log (incorporate our words of the day for bonus points. just kidding):

What helped, and what didn’t? Food business density helped the most, because adding it cut CV RMSE from 10.88 to 10.03. I think it worked because it focuses on whether groceries, corner stores, and restaurants are close enough to reach on foot, which is what makes daily life car-free possible. In contrast, distance to the nearest rail station surprised me most because I expected it to be the strongest feature, but it lowered CV RMSE by only 0.35. In the final model, its coefficient is indistinguishable from zero. Rail stations sit in either the dense core, which renter share and density already describe, or as Regional Rail stops in car-owning neighborhoods like Chestnut Hill. Yet, being near a station doesn’t reliably signal living without a car. Logging food density raised CV RMSE to 9.86, but didn’t do what I hoped for because the commercial storefront corridors in Center City carried more weight that the log compressed.
Read one coefficient twice. I’ll look at food businesses.

β̂ reading suggests that holding the other predictors constant, each additional 100 food businesses per square mile is associated with a car-free share about 2.0 percentage points higher, which is 0.0201 per business per square mile.
ŷ reading suggests that for two tracts identical on every other predictor (one with 100 food businesses per square mile and one with 300) the model predicts a car-free share about 4 points higher for the second.

What’s still missing? The residual map still shows mild underprediction in the far northeast where I suspect are tracts where every predictor points to car ownership. Yet, some households don’t have a car. In the future, I’d want to measure where subsidized and senior housing is located, since a concentration of low-income/older residents who don’t drive can raise a tract’s car-free share without changing density or transit access much. HUD or the City of Philadelphia likely publishes property-level data and I could find a 2023 version after I confirm which tracts the underpredictions fall in.

4.How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? There is likely to be a significant share of it. In running sqrt(mean((tracts$y_moe / 1.645)^2)), the outcome’s typical standard error is about 6.4 percentage points. Squaring that against the final CV RMSE of 9.41 means sampling noise in the ACS estimates could account for nearly half of the model’s squared error. Setting the noise aside leaves about 6.9 points of error that the model could still reduce. The last plot shows that the largest misses (20 to 28 points) are in tracts with CVs between 10% and 40%, where the estimates are fairly precise. Least reliable tracts don’t seem to have unusually large misses. Noise limits how accurate any model can be, but the largest errors emerge between places that my predictors don’t measure.
